“Marvin!” our uncle exclaimed with a smile, “How are you? Will you be coming to the bris?”

“Well now, I wanted to tell you that I’m sorry I can’t make it. The morning hours just ain’t easy for me. But Rabbi, I got a question for you. From where are you gettin’ a mohel? We ain’t got no mohel in S. Antonio.”

“You’re right, Marvin. We’re flying someone all the way from Los Angeles.”

“Rabbi,” Mr. Vexler said, “I would like to have the honor of paying for the mohel.” He went

a donation that was big enough to pay for the mohel’s expenses and even for part of the bris!

Our uncle couldn’t believe his ears. “Wow Marvin! Thank you so much!” Full of joy, he said goodbye and hung up.

Turning back toward the fax machine, our uncle was amazed to see that his letter to the Rebbe had just gone through. At exactly the moment he had asked for a bracha, the Rebbe sent him a clear answer.

Our uncle put the letter in the fax machine and pressed “send”. At that moment, the phone started to ring.

Two years after moving on shlichus to S. Antonio, Texas, our uncle and aunt welcomed a new baby into their family.

As our uncle began planning the bris, he realized that he had a problem. You see, the closest mohel, who lived three hours away in Houston, was out of town and wouldn't be able to come.

The next-closest mohel lived far away in Los Angeles, California. To purchase such a last-minute plane ticket would cost a lot of money.

I can barely pay for the seudah for the bris, our uncle worried. How will I also pay for such an expensive plane ticket?

But there was no other choice. He booked the flight for the mohel and hoped for the best.

Two days before the bris, our uncle was teaching at the community day school, and invited everyone to the simcha. Then, he went back to his office and sat down heavily on his chair. This bris is costing me much more than I expected, he sighed. Where will I get the money from?

Finally, he decided to write to the Rebbe. After telling the Rebbe about the new baby, he asked that everything should happen b’shaah tova umutzlachas. He also described the big expenses of the bris, and asked for a bracha to find enough money to pay for it.

Our uncle then walked over to the fax machine to send the letter to the Ohel. He put the paper in the slot, hit “send”, and watched the paper slowly go inside the machine.

“Rabbi? How ya doin’?” It was Mr. Marvin Vexler, a generous man with a lively personality. A real Texan, he would wear a big cowboy hat and cowboy boots.

Submitted by Yisroel, 10 Avremel, 7 Yakov Tauber, 7 LEC Boys, Miami, Florida
